title: Breaking Certified Defenses: Semantic Adversarial Examples with Spoofed Robustness Certificates
authors: Amin Ghiasi, Ali Shafahi, Tom Goldstein

pages.title: When the Certificate Lies
pages.subtitle: Provable robustness that proves the wrong thing

blocks.html: Certified defenses promise something heuristic defenses cannot: a mathematical guarantee that no adversarial example exists within a given distance of the input. For each prediction they emit a certificate — a radius inside which the label is provably stable.

But a guarantee is only as meaningful as its assumptions. Certificates are proven against a specific threat model — usually small perturbations bounded in an $\ell_p$ norm (every pixel changes by at most $\epsilon$). The certificate says nothing about perturbations outside that ball.

This paper's punchline: you can produce inputs that are visibly, semantically altered (different color, slightly shifted) yet still arrive with a valid robustness certificate. The math is correct; the guarantee is just irrelevant to how the image actually changed.
A certified classifier guarantees its prediction is constant within an $\ell_p$ ball of radius $r$ around the input. Formally, the certificate is a promise of the form:

In words: for every perturbation $\delta$ whose size is at most $r$ in the $\ell_p$ norm, the prediction does not change. This is genuinely proven — there is no white-box or black-box attack inside that ball.

The hidden assumption is the choice of $\ell_p$ and the meaning of 'size'. An $\ell_p$ ball measures change pixel by pixel. But many perturbations that humans perceive as 'the same object' move every pixel by a large amount: shift the whole image one pixel right, or rotate the hue. These live far outside the certified ball, so the certificate makes no claim about them.

The flaw the paper exploits is the gap between perceptual similarity (does it still look like the same scene to a person?) and $\ell_p$ distance (did the pixel values stay numerically close?). The two are not the same.

pages.title: Semantic Perturbations Outside the Ball
pages.subtitle: Change the image in ways the norm ignores

blocks.html: Instead of adding pixel noise (which the certificate is designed to resist), the attacker applies semantic transformations — changes that preserve the object's identity to a human but move the pixels a lot in $\ell_p$ terms, landing well outside the certified ball.

items: Color / hue shifts: recolor the whole image (e.g. rotate hue in HSV). A person still recognizes the object; pixel values change enormously.
Spatial shifts and translations: move the image by a pixel or two. Perceptually trivial, but a large $\ell_p$ distance because every edge moves.
Other identity-preserving edits that the $\ell_p$ threat model never anticipated.

blocks.html: The attacker optimizes the parameters of such a transformation to (a) cause a misclassification while (b) the perturbed image still receives a valid, non-trivial certificate. The result is a semantically adversarial example that the defense itself vouches for.

blocks.tex: x' = T_{\theta}(x), \qquad \| x' - x \|_{p} \gg r \quad \text{yet} \quad x' \; \text{is certified}

blocks.html: Here $T_\theta$ is a semantic transformation (color, shift) with parameters $\theta$. The crafted $x'$ sits far outside the original certified ball, so the certificate computed at $x'$ describes a different, irrelevant neighborhood and says nothing about the visible change that was actually made.

pages.title: How the Certificate Gets Spoofed
pages.subtitle: A true theorem about the wrong neighborhood

blocks.html: It is important to see that nothing in the certificate's proof is broken. The certifier honestly computes: 'around this input $x'$, all $\ell_p$ perturbations up to radius $r$ keep the label.' That statement remains true.

The deception is in what the certificate is silent about. The semantic edit that produced $x'$ from the original $x$ is not an $\ell_p$ perturbation within $r$; it is a large, structured move the proof never covered. So a user reading the certificate at face value — 'this prediction is provably robust' — is misled about the image's actual provenance.
A correct proof about an irrelevant ball is still a misleading guarantee. Robustness is only meaningful relative to a threat model that matches real-world perturbations.

Concretely, the attacker searches over transformation parameters $\theta$ to find a visibly altered image that the network both misclassifies and certifies as robust — producing the paradoxical artifact of a confidently 'certified' wrong answer on an obviously edited picture.

pages.title: Certified and Wrong at the Same Time
pages.subtitle: Demonstrating spoofed certificates

blocks.html: The authors show that common certified-defense pipelines can be made to issue valid certificates for semantically perturbed images that are misclassified. The certificate radius is real and non-trivial; the image is plainly recolored or shifted; the prediction is wrong. All three at once.

This exposes a false sense of security. A practitioner who trusts 'certified robust' as a blanket safety label can be fooled by any adversary willing to step outside the $\ell_p$ box — exactly the moves a real attacker would prefer, since semantic edits survive printing, cropping, and recompression.

pages.title: The Lesson for Provable Defenses
pages.subtitle: Match the threat model to reality

blocks.html: The paper is not an argument against certified defenses — it is a warning about interpreting them. A certificate is a conditional promise: 'safe, assuming the only attacks are small $\ell_p$ perturbations.' If that assumption is wrong, the promise is hollow.
Robustness certificates are only as trustworthy as their threat model. Certifying against $\ell_p$ noise does not certify against color, geometry, or any perturbation the norm cannot see.

The constructive takeaway is to broaden threat models: certify against semantic transformations (color, rotation, translation) directly, and report clearly which perturbations a certificate does and does not cover. Otherwise 'provably robust' becomes a marketing phrase rather than a guarantee.
